title: Docker Builds Slow? Cache Layers Fix It 🐳
ig_caption:
Why did your Docker build jump from 3s to 3m? ⚡
It’s usually “cache busted”… not your CPU.

Under the hood:
- Docker builds images in ordered steps (layers).
- Each layer is cached by its exact inputs (commands + files).
- If step N changes, Docker must rebuild step N… and every layer below it.
- So at 0s: build starts → “CACHE BUSTED ✗”
- Then you’ll see: 0 layers reused → later “3 layers reused ⚡” when prior steps still match.
- Rule of thumb from the visual: put rarely-changing steps first.

Practical takeaway:
- Reorder your Dockerfile so dependencies install earlier (and only app code changes later).
- Keep stable inputs (lockfiles, pinned versions) to maximize cache hits in CI.

Question: What’s the #1 thing in your pipeline that accidentally invalidates Docker cache?
fb_caption:
Docker’s layer cache is one of the biggest levers for reducing build latency in CI/CD—but it’s also a common source of “why is this taking forever?” incidents.

What’s happening architecturally:
- Dockerfile instructions are transformed into layers.
- For each instruction, Docker determines whether a cached result can be reused by comparing the instruction plus its relevant build context inputs.
- When a layer’s inputs change, Docker invalidates that layer and all subsequent layers that depend on it (i.e., “all below rebuild” in the mental model of the reel).

Trade-offs to consider:
- Faster builds vs. determinism: Aggressive cache reuse can hide issues if your inputs aren’t truly stable. Pin versions and use lockfiles to keep builds reproducible.
- Cache efficiency vs. security/compliance: Some orgs prefer clean builds to reduce the risk of stale artifacts. The solution is often targeted caching (e.g., dependencies) rather than disabling cache entirely.
- CI scalability: Local cache is fragile in distributed runners; for consistent speedups, consider registry-backed cache (BuildKit/inline cache) so cache survives across runners and nodes.

Production resilience benefits:
- Shorter build times reduce pipeline queueing and improve deployment throughput.
- More predictable dependency-layer caching lowers variability between runs, which helps incident response and rollback planning.

Actionable best practice:
- Structure Dockerfiles so rarely-changing steps occur first (system packages, dependency installs) and frequently-changing app code last.
- Ensure “cache bust” triggers are intentional (e.g., copy only lockfiles before dependency install, then copy the rest of the source).

If you’re seeing 3 minutes instead of 3 seconds, it’s rarely “Docker is slow”—it’s usually an instruction ordering or input mismatch invalidating the cache. Where in your Dockerfile/CI pipeline do you suspect the first cache invalidation happens?
threads_caption: Docker “cache busted” → every dependent layer rebuilds. Put stable steps first (deps), app code last. Fast builds aren’t luck—they’re Dockerfile structure. What in your setup most often invalidates cache? 👀
